timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hi, I'm Lauren Stern. Hi, I'm Vivian Tron. And we are KnifeGrid students in
Miss Andrew's seventh period Biology Honors class. The question that we received
from the middle school students was how do freshwater salmon survive in the ocean?
Freshwater salmon has been most of their life in the open ocean, living in the
Northern Atlantic Ocean and the Pacific Ocean. They are an adromus, meaning that
most types are born in freshwater and then they migrate to the sea and then
return to freshwater to spawn. As adults, they lay their eggs and gravel beds at
the upper reaches of freshwater streams. And when the eggs hatch, the salmon
spends several months migrating downstream to the open ocean where they
remain for some three to five years. When mature, the adult salmon return to the
mouth of the stream where they originally hatched and migrate upstream to
its head waters, spawn and die. While in freshwater, the fish are hypertonic
to their surroundings. This means that their cells have a lower water concentration
than the surrounding freshwater. Without certain adaptations, the cells would
absorb so much water during oxmosis that the pressure would build up and the
cell would burst. While the salmon are in salt water, they are hypotonic to
their surroundings. That means that their cells have a higher water concentration
than the surrounding sea water. Sea water is made up of the salt which is
dissolved into the solvent water. This ultimately means that the ratio of salt to
water is greater than the ratio of salt to water in freshwater. Without certain
adaptations, the water would leave the salmon cell and the salmon cell would
ultimately shrink and its contents would also be compressed, making it harder for
the cell to carry out certain functions. And this happens through the process of
oxmosis as too much water has left the cell to dilute the salt water outside of
it. In freshwater, the freshwater will move into the cell because the membrane is
permeable only to water and instead of salt moving out, water moves in.
In salt water, water would move out of the cell in an attempt to create an
exotonic concentration on both sides which means that the concentrations of salt and
water are the same on both sides of the membrane. In order for salmon to stay
hydrated well in salt water, the salmon drink sea water to replace the water that
they've already lost. However, a consistent problem occurs where the salmon must
filter out the salt so that it doesn't affect their cells. One of the salmon
salt water adaptations includes the kidney's ability to produce concentrated
urine. This means that the fish can get rid of large amounts of salt while
using minimal amounts of water. The fish contain a special enzyme in their
gill that uses energy from breaking apart molecules to actively transport salt
against their concentration gradient out of the blood and into the salt water.
In summary, while salmon are in freshwater, they can see a large amount of
freshwater which must be diffused into their bloodstream biosmosis.
While in salt water, the fish cannot afford to lose any more water. Therefore,
